name: Bias-cut glamour
region: Paris, France, and Hollywood, United States
summary: The long, close evening gown of the 1930s: silk satin cut on the cross grain, so that it drapes and follows the body.

philosophy.core_thesis: Silk cut across the grain drapes by itself, so that the body shows a line with no boning and no pads.
design_principles: Cut the cloth at 45 degrees to the grain, so that it stretches up to 20 per cent.
Drape the pattern on a small wooden doll, 80 cm high, before the full-size cut.
Keep seams to a minimum: a gown needs two to four main pieces.
Let the waist return to the natural line, and let the gown run in a smooth curve over the hip.
Hang the skirt for 24 hours before the hem is sewn, so that the bias settles.
Choose a heavy crêpe or a satin of 70 to 100 g per square metre.
Finish with a cowl neck, a low back or a halter, and no other trim.
anti_patterns: A boxy 1920s tube with a low waist
Cloth cut on the straight grain

silhouette.shape: A long, narrow column that follows the body from the shoulder to the floor, with a flare at the hem.
silhouette.line: A smooth curve over the bust and hip, a bare or low back, and a long hem that floats, with a small train.
silhouette.fit: Close on the body without darts; the stretch of the bias does the fitting.
silhouette.proportion: The waist is at the natural line. The hem reaches the floor at the back and the ankle at the front. The flare at the hem is 1.5 to 2.5 m.
rules: Cut each main piece on the true bias, and join two pieces with a single seam at the side.
Let the cloth hang from the shoulder or the neck, with a halter or a cowl.
Leave out all hard shapes: no pads, no boning, no stiff lining.
Wear the gown over a slip that is cut on the bias in the same silk.
Add one jewel or one flower at the shoulder; keep the cloth plain.

fabrics.rule: Choose a fluid, heavy silk: satin and crêpe de Chine for the gown, chiffon for the sleeve and the scarf, and no stiff lining.

methods: pattern draped on a small wooden doll
single side seam with a French seam
hem hung and sewn after a rest
cowl or halter cut in one with the bodice
construction.closures: A side hook and snap placket, hidden in the seam, or a back that ties; no visible zip.
construction.details: A cowl neck, a low back, a halter strap, a small train, and one flower or one clip at the shoulder.

surface.pattern: Plain, or a very fine pleat; embroidery only as a single motif at the neck.
surface.gloss: Satin at 40–80 GU; crêpe at 10–20 GU; the light moves with each fold.
surface.wear: The bias stretches and the hem drops with age, so a gown is hung to recover; sweat and light mark the silk.

palette.strategy: Plain, pale or deep colours that show the fold: white, ivory, black, and a dark jewel tone.

processes: hand finish in the couture atelier
making.scale: Couture to the measure of the client; film costume houses in Hollywood made the same cut for the screen.
making.signs: Few seams, a hem that floats, a cowl or halter cut in one, and cloth that clings with no boning.

pieces.form: Cowl-neck gown cut on the bias, to the floor
Halter gown with a low back
Day dress cut on the bias with a flared skirt
Long bias skirt that flares at the hem
Chiffon blouse with a draped neck

positive: silk that clings to the floor
hard studio light with soft shadows

canonical_works.work: White satin gown in Dinner at Eight

emotion.target_response: A sense of ease and allure: the viewer sees the silk move and reads a calm, sure and sensual line.

use_cases: a period costume brief for a 1930s film
an evening or bridal gown with no boning
a fashion image prompt for a Hollywood portrait
avoid_when: the brief wants structure and a built shape
the brief wants a short or casual dress
the brief is a 1920s beaded dress

modifiers.how: Add a boned bodice, a full skirt and a petticoat, and use taffeta.
Drop the waist to the hip, cut the hem to the knee, and add beads.

ornament_level.note: The gown is plain: a jewel or a flower is the only ornament.
